messages.author: 6d3f7222550fe21b
messages.subject: jitter in layer() syntax; dotplot
parts:
(Please ignore my post about jitter; it was a rough draft and is too baroque and tangled.)

What do the "width" and "height" attributes of jitter really do? The example below seems to demonstrate that setting these attributes to zero does *not* remove the jitter.

The two tasks attempted in this post are

(1) to make the simplest of dotplots, i.e., for a single continuous variable, and

(2) to jitter this plot so that repeated identical values are visible.

There must be jitter in the meaningless (y) direction but not in the x direction. I thought that the width and height arguments to jitter would do this, but the example below seems to show otherwise.

I use the layer() syntax because that forces me to think carefully about the components of the grammar.

set.seed(1)
# Sort to make it easier to see what we have
DAAT <- data.frame( X=sort(exp(sample(rnorm(20), replace=T))), zero=0)
print(DAAT)
layer2<-layer(
data=DAAT
, mapping=aes(x=X, y=zero)
, geom="point"
, geom_params=list(shape=1)
, jitter_params=list(height=9, width=0)
, position="jitter"
)
# "expand" seems to control the amount of vertical space around the points.
print(
ggplot() + layer2
+ scale_y_continuous(name="", expand=c(0,1), breaks=0, labels="")
)
# Incidentally, how would I get rid of the tick on the y axis?

# If we set both jitter parameters to zero, there should be no jitter
# at all.
layer2<-layer(
data=DAAT
, mapping=aes(x=X, y=zero)
, geom="point"
, geom_params=list(shape=1)
, jitter_params=list(height=0, width=0)
, position="jitter"
)
print(
ggplot() + layer2
+ scale_y_continuous(name="", expand=c(0,1), breaks=0, labels="")
)
# But there is lots of jitter!

# Although the shortcut position_jitter() is documented, I have found
# no documentation for the full general syntax that uses position=jitter.

What is going on? How do I make the jitter in one or both directions zero?

An alternate way would be to explicitly create a jittered y variable, but that seems to contradict the notion that we can explicitly specify a "jitter" component of our grammar of graphics:

DAAT$geetar<-scale(runif(nrow(DAAT)))/3
layer3<-layer(
data=DAAT
, mapping=aes(x=X, y=geetar)
, geom="point"
, geom_params=list(shape=1)
)
print(
ggplot() + layer3
+ scale_y_continuous(name="", expand=c(0,1), breaks=0, labels="")
)

messages.author: affa918ed63b6275
messages.subject: Re: jitter in layer() syntax; dotplot
parts:
Hi,

jitter_param is not defined. instead you can use position_jitter as
you are aware of:

layer2<-layer(
data=DAAT
, mapping=aes(x=X, y=zero)
, geom="point"
, geom_params=list(shape=1)
, position=position_jitter(height=0, width=0)

)
print(
ggplot() + layer2

+ scale_y_continuous(name="", expand=c(0,1))
)

And you can suppress y ticks (and also horizontal grid) by specifying breaks=NA:

layer2<-layer(
data=DAAT
, mapping=aes(x=X, y=zero)
, geom="point"
, geom_params=list(shape=1)

, position="jitter"
)

print(
ggplot() + layer2
+ scale_y_continuous(name="", expand=c(0,1), breaks=NA)
)

--
Kohske Takahashi <takahash...@gmail.com>

Research Center for Advanced Science and Technology,
The University of  Tokyo, Japan.
http://www.fennel.rcast.u-tokyo.ac.jp/profilee_ktakahashi.html

messages.subject: Re: jitter in layer() syntax; dotplot
parts:
Thank you. Is there some rule to govern when one uses the "something_params" syntax and when one uses the "=position_jitter(" type syntax?

For instance, changing the "geom" part of the syntax so that the layer reads

layer2<-layer(
data=DAAT
, mapping=aes(x=X, y=zero)
, geom=geom_point(shape=1)

, position=position_jitter(height=0, width=0)
)
print(
ggplot() + layer2

+ scale_y_continuous(name="", expand=c(0,1), breaks=NA)
)

would seem to be more consistent, but it returns an error.

Setting "breaks=NA" removes both the tick *and* the horizontal line at y=zero. Is there a way to remove only the tick? This would be like saying

axis(2, tick=FALSE)

in traditional graphics.

One workaround is to use the "hline" geom, although the line is not the same as the white "grid" line that ggplot2 naturally draws:

print(
ggplot() + layer2
+ scale_y_continuous(name="", expand=c(0,1), breaks=NA)

+ geom_hline(mapping=aes(yintercept=0))
)

How would one place the above into full layer syntax? Defining

layer3<-layer(
geom="hline"
, stat="identity"
, geom_params=list( mapping=aes(yintercept=0))
)
print(ggplot() + layer2 + layer3)

appears to be incorrect as it draws no horizontal line at all.

messages.author: d588a03e58ea7e7f
messages.subject: Re: jitter in layer() syntax; dotplot
parts:
On 4/15/2011 12:43 PM, Jacob Wegelin wrote:
>
> Thank you. Is there some rule to govern when one uses the
> "something_params" syntax and when one uses the "=position_jitter(" type
> syntax?

Apparently, this syntax is not readily documented (the help page for
layer sends you to the website which is silent on it). It is documented
in the book, page 42. There it lists the arguments for layer as: geom,
geom_params, stat, stat_params, data, mapping, position. So only geom
and stat take their params as a list as a separate argument. position is
either a string or a position_* function. Dive into the source code and
you will find that there are also arguments params, ..., inherit.aes,
legend, and subset

> For instance, changing the "geom" part of the syntax so that the layer
> reads
>
> layer2<-layer(
> data=DAAT
> , mapping=aes(x=X, y=zero)
> , geom=geom_point(shape=1)
> , position=position_jitter(height=0, width=0)
> )
> print(
> ggplot() + layer2
> + scale_y_continuous(name="", expand=c(0,1), breaks=NA)
> )
>
> would seem to be more consistent, but it returns an error.

Right. Because geom and stat are to be strings with their parameters in
geom_params and stat_params while position can be either a string or the
function with params.

> Setting "breaks=NA" removes both the tick *and* the horizontal line at
> y=zero. Is there a way to remove only the tick? This would be like saying
>
> axis(2, tick=FALSE)
>
> in traditional graphics.

Here is a workaround:

layer2<-layer(data=DAAT,
mapping=aes(x=X, y=zero),
geom="point",
geom_params=list(shape=1),
position=position_jitter(height=2))

print(
ggplot() + layer2 +

scale_y_continuous(name="", expand=c(0,1), breaks=0) +
opts(axis.ticks = theme_blank(),
axis.text.y = theme_blank())
)


I set the only break a 0, which puts a major grid line there. Formatting
the ticks and labels is part of the theme system, and so is controlled
with the opts. A downside is that there is a single option for ticks
(axis.ticks) which controls both the x and y axis. You can't theme the
y ticks separate from the x ones. Setting the y text to blank does get
rid of the 0 label.

> One workaround is to use the "hline" geom, although the line is not the
> same as the white "grid" line that ggplot2 naturally draws:
>
> print(
> ggplot() + layer2
> + scale_y_continuous(name="", expand=c(0,1), breaks=NA)
> + geom_hline(mapping=aes(yintercept=0))
> )
>
> How would one place the above into full layer syntax? Defining
>
> layer3<-layer(
> geom="hline"
> , stat="identity"
> , geom_params=list( mapping=aes(yintercept=0))
> )
> print(ggplot() + layer2 + layer3)
>
> appears to be incorrect as it draws no horizontal line at all.

layer3 <- layer(data=data.frame(yintercept=0),
mapping=aes(yintercept=yintercept),
geom="hline")

I figured this out by exploring the layer object returned by
geom_hline(yintercept=1) and by looking at the source code. Apparently,
yintercept must be turned into an aesthetic, which geom_hline does under
the hood. Also note the default stat for hline is "hline", not "identity".


Editorial: I applaud your wanting to understand ggplot2 at the layer
level. It's something I've wanted to do more as well. I've had the
impression that the layer level is the most pure expression of the
grammar, with the geom_* and stat_* built on that for convenience, and
the qplot level obscuring everything but giving people a chance to
transition. However, starting to look at it, I'm beginning to wonder if
I should think of layer (the function) as an implementation detail,
inasmuch as it makes assumptions that the higher level functions
guarantee and it really isn't meant to be called directly. If you
continue down this path, you will have to use the source and understand
how the system is put together at the programming level; also, there is
no guarantee that things won't change. In fact, I know that the
re-write which is happening changes much of how these things are put
together at the lower levels, but is supposed to maintain the "API" of
the geom_* and stat_* levels.

> Thank you. Is there some rule to govern when one uses the
> "something_params" syntax and when one uses the "=position_jitter(" type
> syntax?
>
>
> Apparently, this syntax is not readily documented (the help page for layer sends you to the website which is silent on it).  It is documented in the book, page 42.  There it lists the arguments for layer as: geom, geom_params, stat, stat_params, data, mapping, position.  So only geom and stat take their params as a list as a separate argument. position is either a string or a position_* function. Dive into the source code and you will find that there are also arguments params, ..., inherit.aes, legend, and subset
>
>
> For instance, changing the "geom" part of the syntax so that the layer
> reads
>
> layer2<-layer(
> data=DAAT
> , mapping=aes(x=X, y=zero)
> , geom=geom_point(shape=1)
> , position=position_jitter(height=0, width=0)
> )
> print(
> ggplot() + layer2
> + scale_y_continuous(name="", expand=c(0,1), breaks=NA)
> )
>
> would seem to be more consistent, but it returns an error.
>
>
> Right.  Because geom and stat are to be strings with their parameters in geom_params and stat_params while position can be either a string or the function with params.
>
>
> Setting "breaks=NA" removes both the tick *and* the horizontal line at
> y=zero. Is there a way to remove only the tick? This would be like saying
>
> axis(2, tick=FALSE)
>
> in traditional graphics.
>
>
> Here is a workaround:
>
> layer2<-layer(data=DAAT,
>              mapping=aes(x=X, y=zero),
>              geom="point",
>              geom_params=list(shape=1),
>              position=position_jitter(height=2))
> print(
>      ggplot() + layer2 +
>      scale_y_continuous(name="", expand=c(0,1), breaks=0) +
>      opts(axis.ticks = theme_blank(),
>           axis.text.y = theme_blank())
>      )
>
>
> I set the only break a 0, which puts a major grid line there. Formatting the ticks and labels is part of the theme system, and so is controlled with the opts.  A downside is that there is a single option for ticks (axis.ticks) which controls both the x and y axis.  You can't theme the y ticks separate from the x ones.  Setting the y text to blank does get rid of the 0 label.
>
>
> One workaround is to use the "hline" geom, although the line is not the
> same as the white "grid" line that ggplot2 naturally draws:
>
> print(
> ggplot() + layer2
> + scale_y_continuous(name="", expand=c(0,1), breaks=NA)
> + geom_hline(mapping=aes(yintercept=0))
> )
>
> How would one place the above into full layer syntax? Defining
>
> layer3<-layer(
> geom="hline"
> , stat="identity"
> , geom_params=list( mapping=aes(yintercept=0))
> )
> print(ggplot() + layer2 + layer3)
>
> appears to be incorrect as it draws no horizontal line at all.
>
>
> layer3 <- layer(data=data.frame(yintercept=0),
>                mapping=aes(yintercept=yintercept),
>                geom="hline")
>
> I figured this out by exploring the layer object returned by geom_hline(yintercept=1) and by looking at the source code.  Apparently, yintercept must be turned into an aesthetic, which geom_hline does under the hood.  Also note the default stat for hline is "hline", not "identity".
>
>
> Editorial: I applaud your wanting to understand ggplot2 at the layer level.  It's something I've wanted to do more as well.  I've had the impression that the layer level is the most pure expression of the grammar, with the geom_* and stat_* built on that for convenience, and the qplot level obscuring everything but giving people a chance to transition.  However, starting to look at it, I'm beginning to wonder if I should think of layer (the function) as an implementation detail, inasmuch as it makes assumptions that the higher level functions guarantee and it really isn't meant to be called directly.  If you continue down this path, you will have to use the source and understand how the system is put together at the programming level; also, there is no guarantee that things won't change.  In fact, I know that the re-write which is happening changes much of how these things are put together at the lower levels, but is supposed to maintain the "API" of the geom_* and stat_* levels.

On 2011-04-15 Fri 19:42, Hadley Wickham wrote:
> Don't have time to write much in detail, but at this level the design
> is not very pleasing to me and is likely to change in the near future.
> Watch the layers package for future directions, including the move
> from proto to s3.
>
> Hadley

Thank you for your 2011 reply and comment on layer(). What are your thoughts on layer() syntax today?

Am I correct that the move from proto to s3 has not yet taken place?

Per Wickham 2009 page 42, the arguments to layer() are geom, geom_params, stat, stat_params, data, mapping, and position.

Why are coord and scale not arguments to layer()?

Also, page 43 seems to say that "geom" and "stat" are dual to each other. It seems to follow that one only uses one of them. Is this correct?

When you say "the layers package," you don't mean there is a separate package called "layers," right? I find none:

> install.packages("layers")
Warning message:
package οΏ½layersοΏ½ is not available (for R version 2.15.3)
> install.packages("layer")
Warning message:
package οΏ½layerοΏ½ is not available (for R version 2.15.3)
>

I'm giving a presentation on ggplot2 to an audience of biostatisticians. I would like to explain the deep structure, including the use of "layer," hence these questions.

Thanks
